name: Tim Paterson

summary.text: Tim Paterson is the programmer who, at Seattle Computer Products in 1980, wrote QDOS (later 86-DOS), an operating system for the Intel 8086 that reproduced the application interface of Digital Research's CP/M. Microsoft licensed 86-DOS non-exclusively in December 1980 and bought all rights in July 1981 for a reported $50,000, then adapted it for the IBM PC, where it shipped as PC-DOS 1.0. Paterson later worked for Microsoft and has maintained that 86-DOS was his original work.

sources.title: Father of DOS Still Having Fun at Microsoft

facts.claim: Paterson began writing QDOS in 1980 as a stand-in for CP/M on the 8086, copying CP/M's application programming interfaces from published references including the CP/M manual so that software would be compatible.
facts.quote: He copied the APIs of CP/M from references, including the published CP/M manual, so that it would be highly compatible.

facts.claim: Microsoft first obtained a non-exclusive licence to 86-DOS in December 1980 and in July 1981 bought all rights from Seattle Computer Products for a reported $50,000; some accounts give the initial licence fee as $25,000 and the final price as between $50,000 and $75,000.
facts.quote: in July 1981 Microsoft purchased all rights to 86-DOS from SCP for $50,000

sources.title: Father of DOS Still Having Fun at Microsoft

facts.claim: Microsoft ported 86-DOS to the 8088 for the IBM PC and licensed it to IBM, where it shipped as PC-DOS 1.0.
facts.quote: Microsoft licensed QDOS to IBM, and it became PC-DOS 1.0.

facts.claim: Paterson has maintained that 86-DOS was his original work and denied referring to CP/M source code while writing it; Gary Kildall called it theft.
facts.quote: Paterson has maintained that the 86-DOS program was his original work and has denied allegations that he referred to CP/M code while writing it.

openQuestions: The site's '$50,000 QDOS' figure is supported by most accounts but sources vary between $50,000 and $75,000 for the July 1981 purchase.
The sources are mirrored enthusiast histories and a 1998 profile; the Computer History Museum's Paterson oral history would be a better primary source.
